<Section id="explanation" type="explanation" title="Spacing, focus and notes" minutes={6}>

### The forgetting curve

After you learn something new, you forget a large part of it within a day or two, and then the loss slows down. Drawn on a chart, this is the forgetting curve: a steep drop followed by a long, gentle slope. A review at the right moment lifts the memory back up, and after each review the curve becomes flatter, so the memory lasts longer before it needs attention again.

### Spaced repetition

Spaced repetition uses that pattern on purpose. Instead of reviewing a topic five times in one evening, you review it once on each of five different days, with the gaps getting longer: the next day, three days later, a week later, two weeks later. Each review is a recall test, not a re-read. If you answer easily, the next gap grows. If you struggle, the gap shrinks and the idea comes back sooner.

Cramming feels productive because the material is fresh during the session. But most of it is gone a few days later. Spacing the same amount of effort over several days gives memories that last for weeks.

### Focus blocks

Spacing tells you when to review; focus blocks shape how each session runs. A focus block is a fixed stretch of single-task work — for example 25 minutes — followed by a short break of about five minutes. After three or four blocks you take a longer break.

- **Decide the task first.** Write down what the block is for, such as "answer the chapter 2 questions".
- **Remove distractions.** Silence notifications and close unrelated tabs before the timer starts.
- **Stop when the timer ends.** A break keeps the next block sharp, even if you feel you could keep going.

### Notes that are easy to review

Notes are only useful if you can review them quickly. A simple layout works well: a question in the margin, the idea in your own words next to it, and a one-line summary at the bottom of the page. Review new notes on the same day, while gaps are still easy to fill, and then let the spaced schedule bring them back.

</Section>

<Section id="examples" type="examples" title="Examples" minutes={2}>

| Situation | Better approach |
|-----------|-----------------|
| Reviewing a topic four times on Sunday night | One recall test on each of four days with growing gaps |
| Studying for two hours with the phone nearby | Four 25-minute focus blocks with the phone in another room |
| Copying a slide word for word | A question, the idea in your own words and a one-line summary |

</Section>

<Section id="real-world" type="realWorld" title="Real world" minutes={1}>

<Callout type="realWorld" title="A nurse keeps procedures fresh">
Sam works night shifts and must remember rarely used procedures. Sam keeps a deck of recall cards and reviews only the cards due each day, which takes ten minutes. Cards answered easily come back after longer gaps; difficult ones return the next day. Months later the rare procedures are still clear.
</Callout>

</Section>

<Section id="tips" type="examTips" title="Tips & traps" minutes={1}>

<Callout type="examTrap" title="One long session is not spacing">
Reviewing the same topic several times in one evening is still cramming. Spacing means different days with growing gaps.
</Callout>

</Section>

<Section id="summary" type="summary" title="Summary" minutes={1}>

Memories fade quickly at first; each spaced review lifts them back up and flattens the curve. Review with recall tests at growing intervals instead of cramming. Run sessions as focus blocks with breaks and no distractions, and keep notes with a question, your own words and a summary. Tomorrow you take a short practice test and plan what to revisit.

</Section>

<Section id="deep-dive" type="deepDive" title="Scheduling reviews with a card system" minutes={5} optional>

A box-based card system automates spacing: cards start in box 1 and move up a box after each correct answer, and back to box 1 after a miss. Each box has a longer review gap than the one before.

<Diagram
  caption="Card boxes: a correct answer moves a card up to a box with a longer gap; a miss sends it back to box 1"
  code={`flowchart LR
  B1["Box 1: daily"] -->|correct| B2["Box 2: every 3 days"]
  B2 -->|correct| B3["Box 3: weekly"]
  B3 -->|correct| B4["Box 4: every 2 weeks"]
  B2 -->|missed| B1
  B3 -->|missed| B1
  B4 -->|missed| B1`}
/>

</Section>
